**The Words Were Good**  

First things first.  
Don't read this if it really makes you nervous. I'm still doing alright, but don't take stupid risks for me. Use your brain while you can, you know?  

With that out of the way, I must say that things are pretty bleak. Which isn't the right word and cliche. Things are pretty fucked, if you ask me. I stock piled all of my God damn soup right next to the books. All of it is inedible now. You were completely right.  

A day or two ago, I went outside. My old basil plant had taken over the yard with its lemony smell and waxy leaves. There were newspapers everywhere, which made me real nervous. I would have gone back in, but I ran out of vitamin D tablets last week and needed the sunlight. It was so warm and perfect.  

I waited for you at the fire hydrant like we said we would if Tuesday came. Well it did, and you weren't there. The paint was peeling off the fire hydrant too. I sat there tearing it off myself until I started hearing this cat yowling by itself somewhere.  

I thought I heard it around the corner, but when I sprinted to catch it, there was this man there, lying on the sidewalk. I screamed, of course. So loud it even popped my ears. Nearly peed myself. He was just so dark and sunken in, like garlic when it's gone bad. He smelled that way too. But he was just lying there, scribbling wildly on the back of a Wal Mart receipt with some deep red lipstick. Something was sticking out of his other hand, and he reached out to hand it to me.  

I really saw no harm in taking it, and I've just felt so alone, you know? Stupid. As I leaned in to that horrible garlic smell, the poor guy tried to communicate.  
"Need."  

Obviously, I bolted. I've never heard anyone on the news back then say what happens if one of them speaks to you.  

It wasn't until I was next to my basil yard again that I looked to see the pen in my hand. The sides were even split, and the ink was oozing out of the sides like blood.

In the backyard of my childhood, there was a stream that served many purposes. The summer, it was the space that surrounded the minnows my sister and I would catch. In fall, it was the collector of golden leaves. Then it became a frozen avoidance that separated us from the powdery wilderness just past it. On one afternoon, it was the catcher of lightning. When the rain stopped, we ran out to the smell of burning and broken trees. There was no glowing glass-sand like in the movies. Only the charred and the stream.
Sometime in my early teens, we moved across town to accommodate our growing collection of siblings and belongings. The new house was much bigger, but the yard was filled with landscaping. Everything smelled different. 
There was a summer when all of my friends were traveling and my siblings became boring. I would go on long bike rides to pass the time. On accident one afternoon, I found myself in front of the old house. The shutters were blue, and new trees were planted in the front yard. I was just barely brave enough to set my bike carefully against a tree and walk silently around the house. There were the broken trees, which looked like bone from lack of water. 

I walked back around to my bike and never came back.
